items.title: Nutrients and consumer pressure influence coral and microbiome recovery following sequential marine heatwaves
items.author: Alex D. Vompe et al.
items.raw_text: Abstract Current and projected ocean conditions under climate change necessitate an understanding of coral holobiont resilience, factors contributing to host survival during marine heatwaves (MHWs), and how corals can recover after MHWs subside. It is especially important to understand how MHWs may interact with local stressors such as nutrient pollution and overfishing. Here, we used a five-year field experiment to investigate the effects of nutrient enrichment and consumer exclusion on host mortality (percent dead tissue) and microbiome stochasticity (beta dispersion) of three coral species, Acropora retusa , Porites lobata , and Pocillopora spp., following MHWs in Moorea, French Polynesia. Our experiment tracked resident coral colonies and their microbiomes through time and captured two MHWs. The interaction of nutrient enrichment with consumer pressure played a significant, yet coral-specific role in host and microbiome recovery from sequential MHWs. Specifically, after the MHWs and under reduced consumer pressure, A. retusa and P. lobata experienced lower host mortality when subjected to ambient nutrient levels. Under high consumer pressure, A. retusa had lower host mortality when nutrient levels were elevated. However, under low consumer pressure, corals with a history of elevated nutrient exposure experienced higher mortality and microbiome stochasticity. On the other hand, Pocillopora spp. microbiomes were more homogenous under elevated nutrients and consumer pressure. Additionally, a reduction in a dominant P. lobata bacterial symbiont, Parendozoicomonas haliclonae , was strongly associated with increased host mortality during and after the MHWs. Overall, these results suggest that local nutrient inputs and fishing pressure can significantly alter reef recovery from MHWs, despite heat stress masking the impacts of these local-scale factors during MHWs.

extra.gist: Five-year field experiment shows nutrient enrichment and consumer exclusion both influence coral survival and microbiome stability during and after marine heatwaves. Local stressor management directly affects reef resilience in aquarium-relevant ways.

items.title: Non-zooxanthellate coral skeletal phenotype persists under end-of-century ocean acidification at a carbon dioxide vent
items.author: Arianna Mancuso et al.
items.raw_text: Ocean acidification, driven by rising atmospheric CO 2 , lowers seawater pH and carbonate saturation states (Ω), posing a critical threat to calcifying organisms, including scleractinian corals. Here, we used a unique CO 2 vent system to explore the long-term effects of chronic low pH on skeletal structure and composition in the non-zooxanthellate solitary scleractinian coral Caryophyllia inornata inhabiting a naturally acidified submarine cave off Panarea Island (Aeolian Archipelago, Italy). Macro-scale skeletal properties (micro-density, bulk density, apparent porosity) were unchanged under acidified conditions, whereas micro-scale structural and compositional features revealed larger crystallite sizes and, in preliminary analyses, higher aspartic and glutamic acid concentrations within the soluble organic matrix (SOM). These results suggest that C. inornata tolerates chronic acidification by maintaining bulk skeletal integrity while adjusting crystalline and organic matrix (OM) features, indicating skeletal plasticity that may sustain biomineralization under projected high-emission ocean acidification scenarios.

extra.gist: Non-zooxanthellate coral (Caryophyllia inornata) maintains normal skeletal structure under acidified conditions at a natural CO2 vent. Some corals show resilience to acidification, shifting expectations for end-of-century survival.

items.title: Indo-Pacific Interactions in the Industrial Era: Insights from Coral Records
items.author: Yunfan Chen et al.
items.raw_text: Abstract The rapid warming of the tropical Indian Ocean and its complex interactions with the Pacific Ocean pose critically important uncertainties as climate warms. However, limited instrumental records challenge investigating decadal and longer-term variations. Here we present four new coral records from Tanzania and combine these with seven published coral timeseries from the western Indian Ocean (WIO) to reconstruct 160-year WIO sea surface temperature (SST). We compare WIO reconstructions with instrumental and coral-based Pacific climate indices to assess Indo-Pacific interactions. Our reconstructions indicate that the WIO cooled slightly in the late 19th century, then warmed by nearly 1°C throughout the 20 th century. This long-term warming correlates closely with increasing El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) asymmetry, characterized by intensified El Niño in the eastern Pacific, transmitting heat to the WIO through ocean-atmosphere interactions. Indo-Pacific interactions also experience decadal modulation, with breakpoints marked by declining WIO-ENSO correlation and reduced ENSO amplitude. After the mid-1970s, El Niño events generate warm anomalies in the WIO associated with a wind anomaly response that transmits the warming into the northwestern Indian Ocean, where it persists into summer. This response was short-lived during the 1960s, with suggestions of alterations in the early 20th century. Comparing our coral reconstructions with Last Millennium CESM1.1 simulations reveals that this model fails to capture key elements of Indo-Pacific interactions — EP SST skewness and decadal modulations in WIO’s response to El Niño. These results suggest that Indo-Pacific interaction mechanisms have changed over the industrial era, but coupled models may not accurately simulate these dynamics.

extra.gist: Four new coral records from Tanzania combined with published WIO data reconstruct 160 years of Indian Ocean temperature, revealing Indo-Pacific climate interactions. Understanding wild reef oceanography illuminates the conditions that shape coral resilience.

items.title: Genome of the precious red coral Hemicorallium imperiale provides insights into the molecular basis of axial skeleton formation in octocorals
items.author: Yanshuo Liang et al.
items.raw_text: Diverse biomineralization strategies of octocorals make these species an important model for understanding the evolution of biomineralization. However, molecular mechanisms underlying biomineralization in octocorals are poorly studied. Precious red corals, which are characterized by their fully calcified axial skeletons and striking red coloration, are ideal for the investigation of the molecular mechanisms underpinning the calcification and pigmentation processes in octocorals. In this study, we generated a high-quality chromosome-level genome of the precious red coral Hemicorallium imperiale. Genomic innovations, including proliferation of long terminal repeats, expansion of metal ion-binding gene families, and rapid evolution of calcification-related genes, are proposed to have played key roles in shaping axial skeleton formation in H. imperiale . Frequent domain shuffling and gene duplications in highly expressed fibrillar collagens may be a common evolutionary strategy supporting the structural diversity of axial skeletons across octocorals. Additional evidence reported in this study, including high expression of chitin-related genes and proteomic data from axial skeleton tissues, suggests that the organic matrix framework containing chitin and fibrillar collagens has deep evolutionary roots and may be a conserved component of ancient biomineralizing systems. Our findings have expanded the current model of the skeletal matrix framework and offer a new perspective into the evolution and diversity of biomineralization.

extra.gist: Chromosome-level genome of precious red coral reveals molecular mechanisms of calcification and pigmentation in octocorals. Genomic insight into octocoral biomineralization advances understanding of soft-coral physiology.

items.title: Divergent temporal variability in calcification and primary production of central Red Sea calcifying macroalgae
items.author: Maggie D. Johnson
items.raw_text: Calcifying macroalgae play critical roles in coral reef ecosystem functioning and carbonate dynamics. However, the metabolic responses underpinning several of their ecological functions remain poorly characterized, particularly in the Red Sea. To evaluate how macroalgal metabolism varies over time under naturally fluctuating conditions, we conducted in situ metabolic assays in the spring and fall over three years (2022-2024) using two ecologically important calcifying reef taxa: the green macroalga Halimeda opuntia and the crustose coralline alga Lithophyllum sp. We quantified rates of light and dark calcification, net photosynthesis, and respiration under natural light and temperature regimes in shallow nearshore habitats of the central Red Sea. Halimeda opuntia metabolism varied significantly across time points in both lagoonal and reef habitats, whereas Lithophyllum sp. showed more stable light calcification rates, though its dark calcification, respiration, and net photosynthesis varied. This variation did not follow a consistent seasonal pattern. Notably, light calcification rates in H. opuntia were more than twice those of Lithophyllum sp., consistent with their roles as fast-growing sediment producers versus slower-growing reef framework stabilizers, respectively. These results provide essential species-resolved in situ metabolic baselines for dominant calcifying macroalgae in the central Red Sea and highlight how divergent macroalgal functional groups contribute to carbonate production and reef stability in a region that regularly experiences environmental extremes.

extra.gist: Study quantifies metabolic rates of two key calcifying reef macroalgae—Halimeda and Lithophyllum—over seasonal cycles in the Red Sea. Understanding their calcification and production underpins nutrient dynamics in reef systems.

items.title: Linking benthic dynamics and herbivore assemblages across a chronically disturbed Caribbean reef
items.author: David Arturo Ortega-Vargas
items.raw_text: Mass coral bleaching events increasingly interact with chronic and acute stressors to reshape tropical reef ecosystems. Caribbean reefs are particularly vulnerable to these cumulative effects, as recurrent thermal stress acts on ecosystems already transformed by disease, coral mortality, and local and regional stressors. Here, we evaluated spatial and seasonal variation in benthic communities and their associations with herbivore assemblages across eight back- and fore-reef sites in Parque Nacional Arrecife de Puerto Morelos (PNAPM), Mexican Caribbean, during the dry, rainy, and cold-front seasons of 2024. Benthic communities differed substantially among sites, with turf algae–sediment matrix and fleshy macroalgae dominating much of the reef system and hard-coral cover remaining generally low. Benthic composition varied significantly among seasons, with a reef zone × season interaction indicating contrasting seasonal trajectories between back- and fore-reef environments, despite the absence of an overall difference between reef zones. Herbivore assemblages also differed markedly among sites but showed no consistent spatial or seasonal pattern at the community level. Associations between herbivores and benthic composition were restricted to particular functional groups and benthic components, revealing selective and context-dependent herbivore–benthos relationships. Overall, decades of cumulative disturbance have not resulted in a uniform contemporary benthic state in Puerto Morelos. Instead, contrasting benthic configurations persist and reorganize seasonally, while their relationships with herbivore assemblages remain context dependent. These findings show that understanding the trajectories of chronically disturbed Caribbean reefs requires recognizing the spatial and seasonal complexity of benthic communities and the context-dependent nature of their relationships with herbivores

extra.gist: Study of benthic community and herbivore interactions across Caribbean reef sites under thermal and chronic stress. Field data on coral-algae-grazer dynamics informs tank management.

items.title: Outplanting laboratory-cultivated Ericaria amentacea germlings at Gyaros Island (Eastern Mediterranean): a 22-month field trial
items.author: Drosos Koutsoubas
items.raw_text: Marine forests formed by the Cystoseira sensu lato complex are declining across the Mediterranean and active restoration is increasingly promoted where natural recovery is constrained by propagule limitation and persistent degraded states. However, restoration outcomes are often reported simply as overall success or failure, failing to distinguish performance during cultivation, transport and outplanting from biological establishment in the recipient site. Here we assess the field performance of active Ericaria amentacea restoration over 22 months at a site located in the Eastern Mediterranean, a region poorly represented by restoration studies. Laboratory-cultivated germlings were outplanted at Gyaros Island, a recently established Marine Protected Area in the central Aegean Sea. Germlings were monitored over 22 months under warm, oligotrophic and potentially grazing-exposed conditions. The cultivation phase produced viable germlings for outplanting. At deployment, mean cover was 61.8%. Percentage cover declined sharply during the first three months and then reached a plateau, apart from a significant dip in the first winter. After 22 months, 47% of the tiles remained attached and 131 tiles (25% of the initially deployed) still bore E. amentacea thalli. Mean thallus length increased during the first year and followed a seasonal pattern consistent with existing ecophysiological data and the seasonal growth of Cystoseira s.l. Mediterranean forests. Critically, no reproductive structures were observed within the study period, indicating that the restored population had not yet reached reproductive maturity. These findings indicate that the restoration protocol was operationally feasible at this single central Aegean site, but biological establishment, particularly the attainment of reproductive maturity, remained incomplete. Long-term assessments of persistence, growth and fertility are essential before restoration success can be claimed in environmentally constrainin

extra.gist: Laboratory-grown Mediterranean seagrass (Ericaria amentacea) was outplanted and monitored for 22 months, tracking survival from cultivation through field establishment. Restoration outcomes for foundation macroalgae inform what works in active reef recovery.

items.title: Assessing the potential distribution of the endangered coral Polycyathus chaishanensis in Taiwan using environmental DNA metabarcoding
items.author: Yi‐Ling Chiu et al.
items.raw_text: The scleractinian coral, Polycyathus chaishanensis , first discovered in the Chaishan region of southern Taiwan, is an endangered species covered by the Taiwan Wildlife Protection Act (2017). At present, its population continues to decline due to environmental pressures. To develop and implement effective conservation strategies, better understanding of the distribution of this species is essential. However, because of its low population density, P. chaishanensis has been difficult to locate using conventional field surveys. In this study, we conducted an environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding survey for scleractinian corals to assess the possible distribution of P. chaishanensis in Taiwan. Surface seawater was collected at 35 coastal sites along the main island of Taiwan and surrounding offshore islands. Coral eDNA were detected by PCR amplification of mitochondrial 12 S rDNA fragments followed by amplicon sequencing. An eDNA-based dataset of scleractinian corals at 35 coastal sites in Taiwan was developed and putative P. chaishanensis -derived eDNA signals were detected at 13 sites, including several locations with previous records of this species. Notably, putative P. chaishanensis -derived eDNA signals were also detected at multiple sites where the species had not been previously reported, suggesting that its distribution may be broader than currently recognized. Although direct field verification at these suggested sites will be required in the future, this study provides new insights into the potential distribution of P. chaishanensis in Taiwan based on eDNA metabarcoding. The information obtained through our eDNA-based surveys will enable more targeted ecological surveys and provide a valuable foundation for the future monitoring, conservation, and restoration of this endangered coral.

extra.gist: Environmental DNA metabarcoding maps the distribution of an endangered Taiwanese scleractinian coral difficult to locate by conventional survey. The technique enables conservation strategies and applies broadly to locating cryptic reef species in the field.

items.title: The Northwest Pacific corals unravel the NPGO- and Victoria Mode-related temperature variability back to the 19th century
items.author: Saori Ito et al.
items.raw_text: Atmospheric and oceanic phenomena in the Pacific Ocean, such as the North Pacific Gyre Oscillation (NPGO) and the Victoria Mode (VM), have significant implications for global climate variability through their linkage with temperature variability in the Central Pacific (CP). The NPGO and VM are defined based on sea surface height and basin-wide sea surface temperature anomaly patterns in the North Pacific, respectively, but their variability is often closely coupled. Although recent studies have drawn attention to their connection with temperature variability in the CP, the historical variability of this connection remains poorly understood due to limited instrumental observations. Because coral Sr/Ca records are primarily sensitive to temperature variability, they can capture signals of the temperature expression of the NPGO, the VM, or their covariability (i.e., NPGO–VM-related temperature variability). Here, we present a long-term reconstruction of NPGO–VM-related temperature variability based on a coral Sr/Ca temperature proxy from the Northwest Pacific (NWP), covering the period from 1799 to 2014 Common Era (CE). The coral-inferred temperature record closely aligns with temperature variability in the CP, indicating an extra-tropical linkage between temperature variability in the CP and NPGO–VM-related temperature variability in the NWP via an ocean–atmosphere bridge. The reconstructed NPGO–VM-related variability shows a pronounced negative phase (cool conditions in the NWP) during the 1860s–1900s, and a positive phase (warm-temperature in the NWP) during the 2000s–2010s. We also find a significant correlation between temperature variability in the CP and reconstructed NPGO–VM-related variability from the early 20th century to 2014, except during the 1970s–1980s. This relationship re-emerged in the 1990s, strengthened thereafter, and remained significant from the 2000s onward. extra.gist: Coral skeletal records from the Northwest Pacific reveal temperature variability driven by NPGO and Victoria Mode back to the 1800s. Coral paleoclimate records extend understanding of Pacific climate patterns affecting reef systems.

items.title: Coral health and environmental associations in the Espíritu Santo Archipelago, Mexico: A 2023 Assessment
items.author: José Carlos Fernando San Esteban-Belmar et al.
items.raw_text: Introduction: Coral reefs in the Eastern Tropical Pacific are increasingly affected by environmental stressors that may compromise coral health and promote disease. However, the health status of coral communities across the Gulf of California remains poorly understood, particularly within the Parque Nacional Zona Marina del Archipiélago Espíritu Santo, where information on coral health and its association with local environmental conditions is limited. Objective: To characterize the health status of coral communities within the Parque Nacional Zona Marina del Archipiélago Espíritu Santo during 2023 and evaluate its association with environmental variables and ecosystem characteristics across the region. Methods: Surveys were conducted at nine sites within the Parque Nacional Zona Marina del Archipiélago Espíritu Santo using belt transects during SCUBA dives to assess scleractinian coral composition, coral health based on the occurrence of morphological lesions, and benthic composition. Historical environmental data (2004–2024) obtained from satellite imagery included seawater temperature, pH, salinity, dissolved oxygen, chlorophyll a, nitrate, and phosphate concentrations. Associations between environmental and ecosystem characteristics and coral health were evaluated using multivariate analyses and generalized linear models. Results: A total of 3 373 colonies were recorded, dominated by the genera Pocillopora (72.7 %) and Porites (24.2 %). Overall lesion prevalence was 66.1 %, with overgrowth (54.75 %) and skeletal deformities (18.01 %) being the most common categories. Significant spatial differences were found in the occurrence of disease-associated lesions (χ² = 116.44, df = 8, p < 0.001) and non-disease-associated lesions (χ² = 65.26, df = 8, p < 0.001). Disease was mainly associated to tissue color change with bleaching and discoloration as the most frequent lesions, and tissue loss represented by the white syndrome. extra.gist: Coral health survey in the Gulf of California's Espíritu Santo Archipelago documents disease and environmental stress in an Eastern Tropical Pacific marine park. Local coral-health assessment informs regional reef status and conservation priorities.

items.title: 35 Years in the Hobby: Inside Brazil's Ultimate Mixed Reef Display | São Paulo, Brazil
items.author: World Wide Corals
items.raw_text: Vic is back in São Paulo visiting Edson at Sea Life, a local aquarium institution that has been operating in the exact same location for 35 years! Inside sits a stunning 400-gallon mixed reef display that breaks almost every rule in the book - bringing Acropora, soft leathers, gorgonians, anemones, torches, and clams together in absolute harmony. Edson shares his old-school philosophy, a simple approach to reef keeping, and vintage photos from Julian Sprung's visit back in 1997! In this video: • Inside Sea Life's 400-gallon, 10-foot mixed reef display operating in São Paulo, Brazil. • The art of the ultimate mixed reef: Balancing lighting and flow for Acropora alongside softies, torches, and leathers. • 35 years of reef-keeping wisdom: Why keeping equipment simple prevents tank-crashing mistakes. • Maintenance and parameters: Monthly 10% water changes, HW salt, calcium reactors, and homemade fish food blends. • Emergency resilience: How local battery backup panels protect vital circulation during citywide blackouts. At World Wide Corals, we have immense respect for the pioneers of our hobby who have kept marine aquariums thriving for decades. Seeing how international reef keepers like Edson strike a balance across every coral family reminds us that patience, observation, and simplicity are often the most powerful tools in reef keeping. What impressed you most about Edson’s 400-gallon mixed reef - his ability to balance demanding SPS with soft corals, the 35-year store legacy, or his straightforward approach to filtration? Share your thoughts in the comments below! If you enjoyed the video, like, subscribe, and turn on notifications so you don't miss our next reef tank tour, coral spotlight, aquarium walkthrough, or behind-the-scenes look at World Wide Corals. items.title: Monitoreo comunitario en arrecifes coralinos: trayectoria de una brigada en el Parque Nacional Arrecife de Puerto Morelos
items.author: Ana Molina‐Hernández et al.
items.raw_text: Introduction: Community participation provides a mechanism to directly involve local populations in the monitoring, conservation, and management of protected natural areas linked to their territory. In reef ecosystems, where maintaining continuous monitoring programs poses a significant logistical challenge, community monitoring teams can help generate ecological data and strengthen their connection to environmental management. In Mexico, this type of participation has been promoted by CONANP through subsidy programs. Objective: This study documents and analyzes the trajectory of a community monitoring team dedicated to reef monitoring in the Puerto Morelos Reef National Park, examining its organizational evolution, capacity development, and generated ecological data, as well as its contribution to the monitoring and management of the protected natural area. Methods: The study describes the path of formation, growth, and consolidation of the collective, its organizational practices, cooperation with authorities and other organizations, and the biological monitoring strategies sustained over a six-year period. Results: Between 2019 and 2025, the team evolved from an emergent response to Stony Coral Tissue Loss Disease into a platform for continuous observation and rapid environmental response. The monitoring efforts generated reliable data across 13 monitored sites, including eight historical priority sites. The team incorporated new indicators and post-disturbance assessment strategies for hurricanes, bleaching, and diseases, strengthening its technical capacity and networks with authorities, academia, and civil society organizations. The data generated directly influenced management decisions, including the temporary closure of subzones due to bleaching and the activation of post-hurricane restoration actions. extra.gist: Mexican researchers document a community-led reef monitoring program in Puerto Morelos, strengthening local stewardship and generating ecological data. Community participation bridges conservation knowledge and local reef protection.

items.title: Attenuated total reflectance infrared spectroscopy as a potential tool for the identification of illegally traded black corals
items.author: Barbara H. Stuart et al.
items.raw_text: Black corals have long been used to produce decorative objects and in traditional medicine. To mitigate the impact of international trade on these corals, all species in the order Antipatharia are listed in Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora. To control the illegal trade of black corals, there is a need for a presumptive method of identifying genuine black corals as it can be difficult to carry out taxonomic identification by visual observation alone. An investigation of the application of attenuated total reflectance infrared spectroscopy to black coral identification has been carried out. Processed coral objects show consistent recognizable protein spectra. Unprocessed black corals produce more variable spectra, but characteristic protein- or chitin-dominant spectra can be used to identify raw black coral specimens. This non-destructive infrared technique can also be used to quickly distinguish genuine black coral from naturally occurring and man-made black materials that may be used to simulate coral.

extra.gist: Infrared spectroscopy offers a presumptive method to identify illegal black coral trade and distinguish genuine specimens. This tool supports enforcement of CITES protections on threatened Antipatharia species.

items.title: ReefFM-SCS: physics-guided foundation-model-assisted weakly supervised framework for fine and stable coral reef extent mapping in the South China Sea
items.author: Xue Liu et al.
items.raw_text: Coral reef extent mapping remains difficult in shallow, optically complex environments affected by water depth, optical attenuation, benthic mixing, and tidal disturbance. This challenge is acute in the South China Sea, where reefs are highly heterogeneous, manual annotation is costly, and existing global boundary products often lack local precision. We developed ReefFM-SCS, a physics-guided, foundation-model-assisted weakly supervised framework for fine and stable coral reef extent mapping. The framework integrates Allen Coral Atlas priors, bathymetry, the diffuse attenuation coefficient (Kd), spectral indices, and a dual-branch optical/physical-prior segmentation network. Rather than serving as the final segmenter, SAM2 is used only for candidate generation; reef-scale adaptive physical constraints guide pseudo-label construction, while quality-weighted multi-temporal fusion integrates annual predictions from 2016 to 2025. The resulting product represents the multi-year stable geomorphic reef-flat extent across major islands and reefs in the South China Sea with high spatial continuity. Compared with the Allen Coral Atlas baseline, precision, recall, F1 score, and IoU improved from 0.84, 0.86, 0.84, and 0.74 to 0.93, 0.95, 0.93, and 0.88, while the boundary metric increased from 0.22 to 0.53. The resulting product provides a consistent spatial baseline for reef habitat mapping, environmental assessment, and related regional applications.

extra.gist: A new AI-assisted framework maps coral reef extent in the South China Sea with improved precision over global datasets. Better reef mapping supports conservation planning and monitoring in optically complex tropical waters.

items.title: The return of red coral: zoology, fisheries and resource management in French colonial Algeria and post-Unification Italy
items.author: Giorgio Bavestrello
items.raw_text: Red coral (Corallium rubrum) was a major subject of eighteenth-century natural history, but during the first half of the nineteenth century it largely ceased to be an autonomous focus of biological investigation. From the 1860s onwards, however, red coral again attracted considerable scientific attention in France and, particularly, in post-Unification Italy. This study examines the reasons for this resurgence by reconstructing the interaction between zoological research, red coral fishing and public administration. Lacaze-Duthiers transformed a problem arising from the regulation of the Algerian fishery into a comprehensive investigation of red coral biology, which remained the principal biological reference for subsequent Italian authors. Italian research generally developed in a different direction. Ministerial enquiries and commissions increasingly focused on the location and productivity of fishing grounds, the incorporation of fishermen’s knowledge into administrative surveys, the biological and environmental interpretation of the exceptional Sciacca deposits, and the cartographic representation of Sardinian red coral grounds. Responses to declining yields followed three complementary strategies: prospecting displaced exploitation towards newly discovered grounds, rotational harvesting sought to regulate it in time, and coralliculture explored the possibility of actively renewing or establishing productive populations. Recognition of local depletion therefore coexisted with continuing confidence in the wider availability of the resource. In the economic and social context of post-Unification Italy, the recurrent involvement of the State in red coral research illustrates how zoological expertise could be mobilized to investigate and develop an economically important marine resource. extra.gist: Historical study of red coral (Corallium rubrum) research, fishing, and regulation in Algeria and Italy from the 1800s onward. Red coral's role in Mediterranean reefs and its trade history matters, though the focus is historiography rather than current biology.
